title: Voltage, Current, Resistance & Power
summary: Four quantities, one relationship (Ohm's Law) - understand these and most basic circuit behavior follows.
quick_actions: Voltage (V, volts) is electrical "pressure" - the potential difference that pushes current through a circuit. It exists between two points even with no current flowing (an open circuit still has a voltage across the gap).
Current (I, amperes/amps) is the actual flow of charge through a circuit - it only flows when there's a complete path (a closed circuit) for it to flow around.

Resistance (R, ohms) opposes current flow, converting some electrical energy to heat. Everything has some resistance except a superconductor or a perfect (zero-resistance) wire, which doesn't exist in practice.

Power (P, watts) is the rate of energy use/conversion: P = V x I. This is why a high-voltage, low-current circuit and a low-voltage, high-current circuit can deliver the same power very differently - and why "amps kill" oversimplifies a real hazard that actually depends on the combination of voltage, current, path through the body, and duration.
Ohm's Law ties three of these together: V = I x R. Knowing any two lets you calculate the third - see the Ohm's Law Solver in Field Tools for the actual calculation.
more_info: For the calculator itself (enter any two values, solve for the rest), see Field Tools' Ohm's Law Solver - this entry covers the concepts, that tool does the arithmetic.

title: AC Fundamentals
summary: Unlike DC, alternating current reverses direction on a regular cycle - which is exactly why AC voltage/current values need their own way of being expressed.
quick_actions: Direct current (DC) flows in one direction only (a battery, most electronics internally). Alternating current (AC) periodically reverses direction, tracing a repeating waveform - almost always a sine wave for utility power.
Frequency (measured in hertz, Hz) is how many complete cycles happen per second - 60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in most of the rest of the world, for utility power specifically.

RMS (root-mean-square) voltage/current is the AC equivalent of a steady DC value that would deliver the same average power - when someone says "120V AC," they mean 120V RMS, even though the actual voltage is constantly changing and briefly peaks higher than that (about 170V for 120V RMS).

AC is used for power distribution specifically because transformers - which only work on AC - make it easy to step voltage up for efficient long-distance transmission (lower current at higher voltage means less resistive loss in the wire) and back down to a safe level for actual use.

Many electronic devices convert AC to DC internally (a power supply/adapter) because their actual circuitry needs a steady DC voltage to operate correctly - the "wall wart" on a charger is doing exactly this conversion.
more_info: AC circuit behavior gets more complex than DC once you introduce components (capacitors, inductors) whose opposition to current changes with frequency - that deeper topic (reactance/impedance) is covered in the Radio Reference's own transmission-line material for the RF-specific case.

title: Semiconductors: Diodes & Transistors
summary: A diode lets current flow one way only; a transistor uses a small current/voltage to control a much larger one.
quick_actions: A diode is a two-terminal semiconductor device that allows current to flow easily in one direction (forward-biased) and blocks it in the other (reverse-biased) - the basic building block of AC-to-DC rectification and one-way current control.

An LED (light-emitting diode) is a diode that emits light when forward-biased - it still only conducts one way, and like any diode needs a current-limiting resistor in most circuits to avoid drawing excessive current and failing.

A transistor has three elements (emitter, base, collector in a bipolar transistor) and can amplify: a small current/voltage at the base controls a much larger current flowing between emitter and collector - this is the basic mechanism behind both analog amplification and digital switching.

Transistors are classified as NPN or PNP (bipolar) based on how their semiconductor layers are arranged, or as field-effect (FET/MOSFET) types that are controlled by voltage rather than current at the control terminal - different types suit different circuit roles, not one "better" type overall.

Integrated circuits (ICs/"chips") are simply many transistors (and other components) fabricated together on one piece of semiconductor material - the same underlying diode/transistor physics, just at a scale of thousands to billions of devices per chip.

title: Circuit Protection: Fuses & Breakers
summary: Both fuses and breakers exist to fail on purpose, safely, before a wire or component fails unsafely.
quick_actions: A fuse contains a metal element that melts and opens the circuit when current exceeds its rating for long enough - simple, cheap, and reliable, but it must be physically replaced after it blows (never with a higher-rated fuse than specified, which defeats its protective purpose).

A circuit breaker uses a mechanical or thermal mechanism to trip and open the circuit at excess current, and - unlike a fuse - can simply be reset once the problem is cleared, without needing a replacement part.

Both exist to protect the wiring and connected equipment from a fault (a short circuit or overload), not primarily to protect a person from shock - the circuit still has to actually be opened before the protection takes effect, which takes some finite time.

A fuse/breaker rating should match the wiring it protects, not just the load you intend to connect - undersizing nuisance-trips on normal loads; oversizing defeats the protection the wiring itself needs.

A fuse/breaker that trips repeatedly is telling you something real is wrong (an overload or a fault) - repeatedly resetting or replacing it without finding the actual cause risks the exact wiring/fire hazard the protection exists to prevent.
more_info: See the Electrical Safety documents in the Document Library below for the full authoritative treatment of electrical hazard recognition and safe practice - this entry covers the protective-device concept, not complete safety procedure.

title: Switches & Relays
summary: A relay is just a switch that's controlled electrically instead of by hand.
quick_actions: A switch makes or breaks a circuit path mechanically - SPST (single-pole, single-throw) is the simplest form: one circuit, on or off. SPDT, DPDT, and other designations describe how many separate circuits ("poles") and how many positions ("throws") a switch handles.

A relay uses a small electrical control current through a coil to mechanically operate a switch contact (or set of contacts) - this lets a low-power control circuit (a sensor, a small button, a microcontroller) safely switch a much higher-power circuit (a motor, a heater, mains power) without the control circuit ever touching the high-power one directly.

"Normally open" (NO) contacts are open (no connection) until the relay/switch is activated; "normally closed" (NC) contacts are the opposite - closed until activated. The same relay often has both types of contacts available for different uses.

Contact rating (voltage and current) matters as much as coil voltage when choosing a relay - a relay's contacts can be damaged or can weld shut if used beyond their rated switching current, especially with inductive loads (motors, solenoids) that produce a voltage spike when switched off.

A solid-state relay (SSR) does the same job as a mechanical relay using semiconductor switching instead of a moving contact - no mechanical wear or contact arcing, but different failure modes (typically failing shorted rather than open) worth knowing if one is in a safety-relevant circuit.
more_info: Relays are the bridge between simple electrical control and the electromechanical control systems covered more fully in the Circuit Protection, Control, and Measurement manual in the Document Library below.

title: Analog vs. Digital Fundamentals
summary: Analog represents a value as a continuously variable quantity; digital represents it as discrete on/off states.
quick_actions: An analog signal/value can be anything within a continuous range (a dial that can point anywhere, a voltage that can be any value between two limits) - it can represent very fine detail, but is also more susceptible to noise and drift accumulating undetected.

A digital signal/value only ever takes on a fixed set of discrete states - almost always binary (two states: on/off, high/low, 1/0) at the hardware level, though what those states represent (a number, a letter, a color) is built up from combinations of many binary digits (bits).

Binary, octal, and hexadecimal are just different ways of writing the same underlying binary values - hexadecimal in particular is common in computing because each hex digit maps to exactly 4 bits, making it a compact, human-readable stand-in for long binary strings.

Digital signals are more resistant to noise than analog ones because a digital receiver only needs to distinguish "closer to 0" from "closer to 1," not reproduce an exact continuous value - this is a major reason digital systems have displaced analog ones for storage and long-distance transmission.

Real-world physical quantities (sound, light, temperature) are inherently analog - a digital system measuring or reproducing them always involves a conversion step (analog-to-digital or digital-to-analog) at some boundary, which is itself a source of quantization/rounding error, however small.
more_info: For the actual binary/hex/octal number systems and Boolean logic gates behind digital electronics, see the Computing Reference page and the NEETS Number Systems and Logic manual in the Document Library below.
